passage:
Dear Damini,

I haven't written in weeks because I didn't know how to say this. Last Sunday I went to bring the teacher a book and ended up in the private wing. A marble hall, cars I had never seen in the courtyard, and two staff members who quickly shut a door when I came near. The teacher has always told us that owning nothing is freedom.

I cried on the bus home. It felt like losing someone. Then I got angry and told myself I'd throw away everything I learned there, the morning silence, the telling of truth, all of it.

But last night I sat quietly anyway, and the stillness was still mine. So I'm keeping that. It's the person I'm still grieving.

Write back when you can.

Tanvir

qa.q: What did Tanvir go to bring the teacher?
qa.a: Tanvir went to bring the teacher a book.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel on the bus, and what did the anger make Tanvir want?
qa.a: It felt like losing someone, so Tanvir cried, then became angry and wanted to throw away everything learned there.

qa.q: What did Tanvir keep, and why is that wise?
qa.a: Tanvir kept the stillness and the telling of truth, separating the practice from the person, so grief over the teacher does not wipe out every value. 🤍

qa.q: How might Damini feel on reading this letter?
qa.a: Damini may feel concerned and want to comfort Tanvir, since the letter ends by asking for a reply after weeks of silence.

grounding: Tanvir discovers the teacher's luxury and secrets, grieves the image, keeps the truth learned and separates the practice from the person.
